articles.title: The notorious Cameroonian prison with its own record label
articles.summary: New Bell's inmates have become mini stars, recording songs and music videos from the confines of the jail.
articles.content:
New Bell - a notorious prison in Douala, Cameroon - is a city within a city.

The facility has its own "taxis" (inmates who whizz through congested courtyards on foot to hand deliver messages), its own law enforcement (burly prisoners who help stretched guards police the facility) and market (a string of stalls where convicts sell and buy goodies, like fried cassava and beignet pastries).

Basically, the occupants of New Bell have adapted the jail's slack laws to work for them. The clearest example of this spirit is Jail Time Records, an on-site music studio and label making mini stars out of the most talented prisoners.

Empereur, the feared leader of gangs inside and outside of the prison, has amassed 24,000 YouTube views with a music video filmed entirely in prison.

Songs from the inmates have gained fans from as far away as South Africa, the US and Argentina, while earlier this year Jail Time Records put on a huge concert for the prisoners in New Bell's courtyard.

"It's this instrument of resistance… where we can really share friendship, love and our voices can be heard," Steve Happi, the former inmate who co-founded Jail Time Records, tells the BBC's Talking Movies programme.

"We don't think anymore about the four walls - we find the freedom."

The Jail Time Records studio is rudimentary - a small, sweaty recording booth attached to a room inhabited by a solitary computer.

But it is also the site of great catharsis and creativity, as per a recent, acclaimed documentary named after the studio.

Directed by Happi and Italian artist Dione Roach, his Jail Time Records co-founder, it was filmed in New Bell over six years.

Last month it won three prizes, including best documentary feature, at New York's Tribeca film festival.

In the film, a prisoner named Stone raps into the studio's microphone: "Heart of stone, it's war. My senses shatter like broken glass.

"I'm closed and tight like a cell door. No solid ground I slip like a fish."
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful and inspiring initiative within a notorious prison where inmates use music to express themselves, foster creativity, and find emotional freedom. This has a positive real-world impact by promoting rehabilitation and hope among prisoners, with significant cultural resonance as evidenced by international fan engagement and award-winning documentary recognition. The story is focused and provides substantial context about the initiative and its effects.
articles.personality_title: Cameroon's New Bell Prison Creates Stars Through Music
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – New Bell is a well-known prison in Douala, Cameroon. Despite being a tough place, it has its own small world where inmates manage daily life with unique rules and systems.

**What happened** – Inside New Bell, prisoners started Jail Time Records, a music studio and record label. Inmates record songs and music videos, sharing their stories and talents from behind bars. One leader, Empereur, gained 24,000 YouTube views for a video filmed entirely in prison. The label also held a big concert for the prisoners earlier this year.

**Impact** – This music project gives prisoners a way to express themselves and feel free, even in a difficult environment. Their songs have fans not only in Cameroon but also in countries like South Africa, the US, and Argentina. The story of Jail Time Records was captured in a documentary that won three awards at the Tribeca Film Festival, showing how powerful and inspiring this effort is.

**What's next step** – The filmmakers and founders hope to keep supporting the inmates’ creativity and possibly expand the project. The success of the documentary may bring more attention and resources to help prisoners through music.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A prison in Cameroon is turning inmates into music stars, showing how creativity can bring freedom and hope even behind bars.

articles.title: What a week's work experience taught these Year 10s about their futures
articles.summary: Three 15-year-olds tell the BBC how their outlook changed after one week in the world of work.
articles.content:
When Kelsey first arrived at secondary school, she said she wanted to be almost anywhere else but there.

She struggled with friendships, clashed with teachers and often tried to avoid coming into school.

But after a week's work experience placement at Whipsnade Zoo, in Bedfordshire, her outlook could not be more different.

She said it made her a "completely different person" - more confident, with a "good group of friends" and a greater sense of purpose about where her education could lead her.

Children across the UK are strongly encouraged to do work experience while at school. In England, the government published new legal guidance in June for schools to deliver two weeks of "in-person and immersive" work experience in future, one between Year 7 and Year 9, and one between Years 10 and 11.

But not all work experience placements are equal, and finding the right one can be tricky.

Organisations like the Sutton Trust and the Social Mobility Foundation said some students could be limited by the availability of placements in their area, or a lack of family connections with local employers.

BBC News spoke to three Year 10 pupils, one year ahead of their final GCSE exams, about how they decided what areas of work they were interested in, their experiences of trying to find the right placement, and what it taught them about their future education and ultimate career goals.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the positive impact of immersive work experience on young students' confidence, outlook, and future career aspirations, which has broad educational and social benefits. It focuses on a meaningful change in students' lives and the government's supportive policy to enhance work experience opportunities, demonstrating a tangible benefit to youth development and social mobility.
articles.personality_title: A week at work helps Year 10 students see their future differently
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many students in the UK take part in work experience while still at school. This helps them learn about jobs and think about what they want to do in the future. The government has made new rules to make sure students get two weeks of real, hands-on work experience during their school years.

**What happened** – Three 15-year-old students shared how a one-week work experience changed how they feel about school and their future. For example, Kelsey, who used to dislike school and had trouble making friends, said her time at Whipsnade Zoo made her more confident and gave her a clearer idea of what she wants to do. She now has good friends and feels more positive about learning.

**Impact** – This story shows how the right work experience can help students grow in confidence and find new goals. It also points out that not all students have the same chances to find good placements, especially if they don’t have family connections or nearby opportunities. Work experience can make a big difference in helping young people think about education and careers in a practical way.

**What's next step** – Schools will work to give students two weeks of work experience, as the government suggests. Groups like the Sutton Trust and Social Mobility Foundation will keep trying to help students from all backgrounds find good placements. This could mean more young people feel ready and excited about their futures.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Spending time in a real workplace helped these students feel more confident and clearer about their future education and jobs.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une semaine de travail aide des élèves de 4e à mieux voir leur avenir
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup d'élèves au Royaume-Uni font un stage pendant leur scolarité. Cela les aide à découvrir des métiers et à réfléchir à leur avenir. Le gouvernement a mis en place de nouvelles règles pour que les élèves aient deux semaines de stage réel et pratique pendant leur parcours scolaire.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Trois élèves de 15 ans ont raconté comment une semaine de stage a changé leur vision de l'école et de leur avenir. Par exemple, Kelsey, qui n'aimait pas l'école et avait du mal à se faire des amis, a dit que son stage au zoo de Whipsnade l'a rendue plus confiante et lui a donné une idée plus claire de ce qu'elle veut faire. Elle a maintenant de bons amis et voit l'école plus positivement.

**Impact** – Cette histoire montre que le bon stage peut aider les élèves à gagner en confiance et à trouver de nouveaux objectifs. Elle souligne aussi que tous les élèves n'ont pas les mêmes chances de trouver un bon stage, surtout s'ils n'ont pas de contacts ou d'opportunités près de chez eux. Le stage peut vraiment aider les jeunes à penser concrètement à leur éducation et leur métier.

**Les prochaines étapes** – Les écoles vont organiser deux semaines de stage, comme le conseille le gouvernement. Des organisations comme la Sutton Trust et la Social Mobility Foundation continueront d'aider les élèves de tous horizons à trouver de bons stages. Cela pourrait donner envie à plus de jeunes de se préparer pour leur avenir.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Passer du temps en milieu professionnel a aidé ces élèves à être plus confiants et plus clairs sur leur avenir scolaire et professionnel.
articles.personality_title_es: Una semana de trabajo ayuda a estudiantes de 4º de ESO a ver mejor su futuro
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos estudiantes en el Reino Unido hacen prácticas mientras están en la escuela. Esto les ayuda a conocer trabajos y a pensar en lo que quieren hacer en el futuro. El gobierno ha creado nuevas reglas para que los estudiantes tengan dos semanas de experiencia laboral real y práctica durante sus años escolares.

**Qué pasó** – Tres estudiantes de 15 años contaron cómo una semana de prácticas cambió su forma de ver la escuela y su futuro. Por ejemplo, Kelsey, que no le gustaba la escuela y tenía problemas para hacer amigos, dijo que su tiempo en el zoológico de Whipsnade la hizo más segura y le dio una idea clara de lo que quiere hacer. Ahora tiene buenos amigos y una actitud más positiva hacia la escuela.

**Impacto** – Esta historia muestra que la experiencia laboral adecuada puede ayudar a los estudiantes a ganar confianza y encontrar nuevos objetivos. También señala que no todos tienen las mismas oportunidades para encontrar buenas prácticas, especialmente si no tienen contactos familiares o lugares cerca. La experiencia laboral puede cambiar mucho la forma en que los jóvenes piensan sobre su educación y trabajo.

**Próximo paso** – Las escuelas trabajarán para ofrecer dos semanas de experiencia laboral, como sugiere el gobierno. Organizaciones como Sutton Trust y Social Mobility Foundation seguirán ayudando a estudiantes de todos los orígenes a encontrar buenas prácticas. Esto podría hacer que más jóvenes se sientan preparados y motivados para su futuro.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Pasar tiempo en un lugar de trabajo real ayudó a estos estudiantes a sentirse más seguros y claros sobre su educación y trabajo futuros.
